mcq.q: In a contract of guarantee, the person to whom the guarantee is given is the:
mcq.explain: Section 126 names the three parties: the person who gives the guarantee is the surety, the person in respect of whose default it is given is the principal debtor, and the person to whom it is given is the creditor. The creditor is the party protected by the guarantee.
mcq.topic: Contract of guarantee — parties and essentials (Sections 126, 127)
mcq.fast: Given BY surety, FOR debtor, TO creditor.

mcq.q: Which statement about a contract of guarantee is correct?
options: It must be in writing and registered
It must be in writing on stamp paper to be valid
It is valid only if the surety receives payment
It may be oral or written
mcq.explain: Section 126 expressly provides that a guarantee may be either oral or written. Under Section 127, a benefit given to the principal debtor is enough consideration for the surety's promise; the surety himself need not gain anything.
mcq.topic: Contract of guarantee — parties and essentials (Sections 126, 127)
mcq.fast: Guarantee: oral OK (s.126); benefit to debtor = consideration (s.127).

mcq.q: Under Section 128, how far is the surety liable?
options: Always one-half of the debtor's liability
To the same extent as the principal debtor, unless the guarantee limits it
Secondary, arising only after the creditor sues the debtor first
Limited to the interest on the debt
mcq.explain: Section 128 makes the surety liable to the same extent as the principal debtor, unless the guarantee itself says otherwise. The creditor may proceed directly against the surety without first suing the principal debtor, because the surety's liability arises immediately on default.
mcq.topic: Nature and extent of the surety's liability (Sections 128, 132)
mcq.fast: Co-extensive = same extent, and the creditor can go to the surety first.

mcq.q: A guarantee extending to a series of transactions is a:
mcq.explain: Section 129 defines a continuing guarantee as one that extends to a series of transactions. A specific guarantee covers a single debt or transaction and comes to an end when that debt is paid. A running credit account guaranteed up to a limit is a common example of a continuing guarantee.

mcq.q: A surety gave a continuing guarantee for goods supplied to a debtor and then died. In the absence of a contrary contract, his death:
options: Revokes it as to past and future transactions
Makes his heirs liable for all future supplies
Revokes the guarantee as to future transactions — Section 131
mcq.explain: Under Section 131, unless agreed otherwise, a surety's death ends a continuing guarantee for transactions after the death. His estate remains liable for supplies already made before his death, because those debts arose while the guarantee was alive; the creditor should therefore stop fresh credit once he learns of the death.
mcq.fast: Death of surety: past transactions = estate liable; future = revoked.

mcq.q: Without the surety's consent, the creditor and the principal debtor change the terms of the contract. Under Section 133 the surety is:
options: Discharged as to transactions subsequent to the variance
Discharged only if the change reduces his liability
mcq.explain: Section 133 says any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance. He remains liable for transactions before the change.
mcq.fast: Variance without surety's consent -> discharged for later transactions.

mcq.q: Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor, without any agreement:
options: Does not discharge the surety — Section 137
Makes the surety liable for interest only
mcq.explain: Section 137: if the creditor simply holds back from suing the debtor or using other remedies, the surety stays liable, unless the guarantee says otherwise. Only a binding agreement giving time to the debtor (Section 135) discharges him.
mcq.fast: Mere delay (forbearance) ≠ discharge. A binding promise to give time = discharge.

mcq.q: Having paid the guaranteed debt in full, the surety takes over the creditor's rights against the debtor. This right is called:
mcq.explain: Section 140: a surety who has paid everything due from him takes over every right the creditor held against the debtor. This is called subrogation. Contribution is a right among co-sureties, and Section 145 gives him an implied indemnity from the debtor.
mcq.fast: Steps into the creditor's shoes = subrogation.

mcq.q: P, Q and R are co-sureties for a debt of ₹3,60,000 with no agreement between them. The debtor defaults and the creditor recovers it all from P. P can recover from Q:
mcq.explain: Under Section 146, unless they agreed otherwise, co-sureties for one debt share it equally among themselves, whether the whole debt or the unpaid balance. Each bears ₹3,60,000 ÷ 3 = ₹1,20,000, so P recovers ₹1,20,000 each from Q and R.
mcq.fast: Co-sureties = equal shares: debt ÷ number of sureties.

mcq.q: Section 124 indemnity covers loss caused to the promisee by:
options: The conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person
mcq.explain: In Section 124 the indemnifier promises to protect the other party against loss arising from his own conduct or from the conduct of some other person. Under this definition, loss from accidents or acts of God not caused by human conduct is outside the Section.
mcq.fast: Indian s.124 = loss by HUMAN conduct (promisor or another person).
